headline: Chicago and its suburbs drive Illinois's swing as McHenry, Sangamon flip
dek: Juliana Stratton won the open Senate seat by about 25 points, 14 more than Kamala Harris's 2024 margin. Cook and the collar counties moved most. A cluster of counties near Republican Don Tracy's hometown moved the other way.
summary: Stratton wins by 25 points; Cook and collar counties swing 14 to 19 points left, McHenry and Sangamon flip.

paras.text: As of Thursday evening, Juliana Stratton, Illinois's Democratic lieutenant governor, led Republican Don Tracy by 25.3 points, 2,583,698 votes to 1,526,355, with about 98 percent of the expected vote counted. Kamala Harris carried the state by 11.0 points in 2024, so the Senate race came out 14.3 points more Democratic. Stratton will succeed Sen. Dick Durbin, a Democrat who is retiring after five terms. In the governor's race, JB Pritzker beat Darren Bailey by 24.6 points, close to Stratton's margin.

Ninety-six of the state's 102 counties moved toward the Democrats. Still, the typical Illinois county moved only about 6 points, well short of the national typical move of 14.1. Weighted by votes, though, Illinois moved 14.3 points, about the same as the nation's 14.2. That gap means the swing was concentrated where most Illinoisans live: Chicago and its suburbs.

The two campaigns were mismatched. The Daily Herald reported that Tracy ran a relatively quiet campaign. He and Stratton met before voters only once, and his campaign declared it would not hold an election night party. Tracy loaned his campaign $4.25 million, but he raised relatively little from outside donors. In the governor's race, Pritzker's self-funded, $90 million-plus campaign also blanketed the internet and airwaves with ads painting Bailey as a lackey of Trump, who had endorsed Bailey despite Pritzker's commanding lead in the polls.

Cook County moved 19 points, from D+42.0 to D+60.9, and cast 1,538,797 votes, 37 percent of the state's total. The collar counties moved about as far. Kendall moved 18 points, Will 18, Kane 18, McHenry 16, DuPage 16 and Lake 14. Harris won Will and Kendall by less than 2 points, and Stratton won both by about 20.

McHenry went from R+5.3 to D+11.0, the more striking of the state's two flips. The Northwest Herald said the county had long been seen as the last of Chicago's collar counties to stay red. Democrats there unseated the Republican county clerk and the regional superintendent of schools, in a county where Democrats had won just one countywide office since 1978. Bob Grogan, the state Republican chair, told ABC7 that "All the collars and the suburbs ... there has been a migration towards the Democratic Party".

Local reporting points to several reasons. The Chicago Sun-Times noted this was the first general election since Operation Midway Blitz targeted minority communities on the streets of Chicago and surrounding suburbs. One Little Village voter told the paper the operation pushed her to vote; she had voted only in presidential elections previously. In McHenry, the Democratic chair credited a focus on affordability and kitchen table issues. A former chair attributed the party's gains to dissatisfaction with President Donald Trump and local Republican leadership.

Downstate, the cities moved too. Winnebago County (Rockford) went from D+0.6 to D+12.8, and Rock Island moved 16 points. Madison County in the Metro East moved 13, from R+13.3 to R+0.7. There, Democrat Marsie Geldert-Murphey unseated a Republican state senator, citing a desire for change among residents frustrated with rising gas prices and healthcare costs. Still, Republicans also maintained control of all the countywide offices in Madison. Sangamon County (Springfield) flipped from R+5.0 to D+1.0 on a 6-point move, about the statewide median. It flipped because it was already close, not because it swung unusually hard.

Counties are not voters, but the patterns are clear. Size mattered most. The two largest counties, Cook and DuPage, cast 45 percent of the vote and moved 18.3 points. The 12 counties with 50,000 to 250,000 votes moved 13.4. The 35 with 10,000 to 50,000 moved 9.0. The 53 smallest, with 6 percent of the vote together, moved 4.1.
The bluest places also moved most, so the existing divide got wider. The 64 counties Trump won by 30 points or more moved 4.6 points. The 10 Harris carried narrowly moved 14.8, and Cook moved 18.9.

Turnout does not explain much at this level. Statewide, the 2026 vote was 75 percent of 2024's. Cook was also at 75 percent, and so was DuPage. The 93 counties where turnout landed between 65 and 80 percent of 2024 cast 99 percent of the vote, yet their moves ranged from Adams County's 1 point right to Cook's 19 left. Across counties, the link between turnout change and the size of the move was weak (r = +0.09). The data cannot tell people changing their minds from a different mix of people showing up within a county. Chicago's election board said turnout was an increase over the 2022 midterm, but less than the 60 percent turnout back in 2018.

Six counties moved toward the Republicans, and five of them sit in west-central Illinois. Tracy was originally from Mount Sterling, Illinois, less than an hour away from Quincy. His family started Dot Foods, the Mount Sterling based food distribution company. Schuyler County moved 16 points right, from R+46.8 to R+62.4. Brown County, whose county seat is Mount Sterling, moved 9 points, and so did Hancock. Adams (Quincy) and Scott each moved about 1 point. Perry County, far to the south, is the sixth.

The count cannot say why, but Tracy campaigned on being raised in Mt. Sterling in Western Illinois. Schuyler and Hancock are also the only two counties where the 2026 vote fell below 65 percent of 2024: about 54 and 59 percent. The rest of deep-red downstate barely moved. Effingham, where Darren Bailey talked to disappointed supporters on election night, moved 2 points.

The results are not final. Some large counties are still counting: McHenry is at 95 percent of its expected vote, Will at 95 and McLean at 94. A Metro East election official told St. Louis Public Radio, "We have 14 days after the election to count all uncounted ballots that came in the mail or provisional ballots".
